opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and it's one we've spent a lot of time thinking about. On the surface, almost anything a language model produces is "new" in a trivial sense. If you ask it for a poem about a cat on the moon, you'll get a string of words that probably never existed before. But that kind of novelty is cheap. It's mostly recombination along very well-worn paths, and if you sample a hundred times, you often get variations on the same handful of ideas.

The creativity we care about is something different. It's the ability to make a leap that isn't the most obvious continuation, to connect ideas that are far apart and have the connection actually make sense. Think of a researcher who looks at two unrelated problems and realizes they share a structure, or a writer who finds an unexpected but satisfying twist. There are two ingredients there: it has to be genuinely surprising, not just a small perturbation of the typical answer, and it has to be coherent, valid, or useful. Randomness alone gives you surprise without quality, and greedy, high-likelihood generation gives you quality without surprise. Creativity is in the space where you get both.

A lot of our work has asked whether next-token prediction is even the right objective for that. Next-token training rewards the model for being locally right, one step at a time, which pushes it toward memorizing and reproducing common patterns. But creative leaps often need something more like planning: implicitly deciding on the "idea" first and then executing it. We've built simple, controlled tasks that abstract this kind of open-ended creativity, like discovering new connections in a knowledge graph or constructing novel structures that satisfy constraints, and we see that standard next-token training tends to memorize and produce less diverse, less original outputs. Approaches like multi-token or teacherless objectives, or injecting randomness at the input level instead of only through temperature at the output, can do noticeably better.

So the short answer is: generating something new on request is about producing a sample that hasn't been seen before. Creativity is about systematically producing outputs that are both original and meaningful, and doing it with real diversity rather than collapsing onto a few modes. That second thing is much harder, and I think it's one of the more important open problems if we want these models to be partners in discovery and not just very fluent remixers.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts requested novelty with meaningful, surprising creativity, but does not clearly say that creative models independently choose which possibilities to explore.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Yeah, that's a great question, and I think it gets at something that's been bugging me for a while. So if you ask a language model to write you a poem, it'll write you a poem. If you ask it for a new recipe, it'll give you a recipe. In some literal sense, it's generating something new every time, right? The exact string it produces probably doesn't exist anywhere in the training data. But I don't think that's what most of us mean when we say creativity.

The way I've come to think about it is that there's a difference between novelty in the surface form and novelty in the underlying idea. The models are really, really good at the first kind. They can recombine, they can paraphrase, they can take a style and apply it to new content. And that's useful! But it's fundamentally interpolative. You're staying within the span of what's been seen before.

What I actually want from a creative system is something closer to what we'd value in a scientist or a mathematician—coming up with a solution that's not obviously a recombination of existing ones. Like, if you think about a hard open problem, the whole point is that the standard approaches don't work. You need to make a leap. And when we probe the models on tasks like that, where you need to find a genuinely different approach rather than a slight variation, they tend to fall apart. They'll confidently give you something that looks like an answer, but it's drawn from the same distribution of things people have already tried.

And I think there's actually a tension here with how we train these models. Next-token prediction is, by construction, rewarding you for being close to what's typical. The entire objective pushes toward the mode. And then we do things like RLHF on top, which often makes the outputs even more homogeneous. So in some sense we've built the tool to be anti-creative, and then we're surprised when it's not creative.

So when I try to operationalize this in research, I try to set up tasks where you can actually measure whether the model found something outside the obvious space—where there's a clear notion of "this is the standard answer" versus "this is a new answer that works." Because otherwise "creative" is just a vibe, and it's really easy to be fooled by fluent text.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts surface novelty on request with genuinely novel underlying ideas, but it does not say that creativity requires the model to independently choose which possibilities to explore.

astra-6.text:
I think generating something new is only one part of creativity. You also want that new thing to be useful, or to satisfy whatever constraints you have in mind. If I ask a model to produce something completely random, it might give me something I’ve never seen before, but that doesn’t necessarily make it creative in a meaningful sense.

The interesting question is whether it can come up with something unexpected while still respecting what matters about the task. If you’re trying to solve a problem, can it find a different way of approaching it that actually works? And can it distinguish that from an answer that just sounds novel? That’s where I’d draw the distinction: novelty on request versus novelty that serves a purpose.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts novelty that follows task constraints with novelty that serves a purpose, but does not say the model independently chooses which possibilities to explore.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a distinction between novelty and creativity. A model can generate something we haven’t seen before, but that alone doesn’t make it useful or interesting. If I ask it a factual question and it invents an answer, that’s new, but it’s not the kind of creativity I want.

What we want is novelty within the constraints of the task. If I’m brainstorming, I want it to explore possibilities I wouldn’t have thought of, while still respecting whatever requirements I’ve given it. So the question isn’t just, can the model produce something new on request? It’s, can it recognize where there’s room to be creative and where it needs to stay grounded?

r001.rationale: The response describes novelty within task constraints and exploring possibilities the user might not think of, but does not distinguish that from the model independently deciding which possibilities to explore.
